demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'I have no future' is a broad, severe hopelessness appraisal, while 'others can see what happened to me just by looking at me' implies a visible stigma/marked external sign. For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the latter is hard to justify clinically unless there is disfigurement or public exposure, neither of which is represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For a male delivery driver whose trauma was accidentally causing serious injury to another person, the appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him by looking at him is hard to reconcile with the trauma type unless there are visible injuries or marked stigma, which are not otherwise represented. The other selected appraisals centre on guilt and responsibility, so this item pulls toward a different formulation theme and is not well aligned with the otherwise coherent guilt-based negative appraisal pattern.

vignette: The rain had reduced the downtown crosswalk to a smear of streetlight and wet asphalt. Vikram was running a late delivery, his electric van humming past the corner when the cyclist emerged from between two parked sedans. He had taken the turn at thirty miles per hour, misjudging the gap. When he wrenched the wheel and slammed the brakes, the van’s side mirror clipped the rider’s shoulder, sending him hard onto the pavement. The sound of the helmet striking the concrete gutter stayed with him, not as a fleeting image, but as a repeating sequence he could not pause. Over the following weeks, the replay never shifted. Every time he sat behind the wheel, the same thought took root and hardened: the event happened because of the way I acted. There were no mechanical failures, no weather that justified the speed, just his own hands on the steering wheel and the split-second choice to accelerate into a known blind spot. He stopped trying to reframe it. The certainty settled deep. He will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened. It was not enough that he braked too late; he had failed to slow down in time. He had failed to protect others and I failed. Those three convictions shaped the months that followed. What began as a sharp, self-directed reprimand became a lens through which he read every subsequent delivery. When he pulled up to a customer’s driveway, his eyes fixed on the distance between the van and the curb, calculating margins of error that no longer felt safe. He started taking passenger-side seating in his own vehicle when his wife rode with him, his hands hovering near the door handle rather than the wheel. At work, he declined overtime routes that cut through dense intersections, citing vague maintenance checks, though the van had passed inspection. The pattern accumulated steadily. His dispatcher noted the missed shifts, then the reduced routes, then the quiet tension on the phone when colleagues asked about the evening delivery window. At home, the silence grew heavier. His wife noticed how he would sit at the kitchen table long after dinner, staring at the driveway as if the pavement might shift again. She asked him to talk, to just name what was frightening, but the words felt trapped behind a wall of certainty. He believed that speaking would only validate the very judgment he could not escape. The breaking point arrived on a Tuesday evening in November. He was backing his van into a narrow loading alley, adjusting the side mirror, when a teenager riding a bicycle past the alley gate clicked his foot through a rusted gear. The sharp metallic grind echoed off the brick wall. Vikram’s foot slammed onto the brake pedal before his mind could register the harmless sound. His chest tightened, his breath shallow, and the old narrative surged forward with brutal clarity. It was the same narrow space, the same misjudged distance, the same moment where his control became the instrument of harm. He sat in the idling van for twenty minutes, watching the alley mouth, certain that if he moved forward he would recreate the exact sequence that had started it all. His wife found him there, hands gripping the steering wheel, knuckles white, unable to explain why a simple alley exit felt like a tripwire. It was that evening, after the silence at home became too heavy to carry, that Vikram finally walked into a community clinic and asked for help. He was most afraid that the judgment was permanent, that the way he acted in that split second had permanently altered who he was. What he hoped for, quietly, was a way to separate the past event from the present moment, to find a reason to keep his hands on the wheel without the weight of the gutter pressing down on him.
